612.quote_or_event: “In every affair consider what precedes and follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit; but not having thought of the consequences, when some of them appear you will shamefully desist.”
612.explanation: Epictetus warns that people who start eagerly without weighing the effort required give up in disgrace when difficulties appear, and compares them to children who play at one role after another but are nothing with their whole soul.
612.tie_back: Both texts call it shameful to drop a task halfway, though Epictetus places the remedy in weighing the work before starting rather than in keeping one's effort up once started.
612._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter translation). Strong match on the disgrace of abandoning work begun; Epictetus stresses prior deliberation, the Kural stresses not slackening midway, and the Kural's point that the world abandons such people is absent.

687.quote_or_event: Socrates tells Phaedrus that a true speaker must first learn the different kinds of soul and which kinds of speech persuade each. He must then be able to recognise them quickly in real life, and must add to this a knowledge of the right times for speaking and for keeping silent before his art is complete.
687.explanation: In the closing discussion of rhetoric, Plato makes knowledge of the listener, together with a sense of the right moment (kairos) for each kind of speech, a condition of any real art of persuasion.
687.tie_back: Plato's speaker, like the Kural's ideal envoy, must judge the audience and the moment before choosing his words.
687._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; this section could not be loaded verbatim in this session (the MIT and Perseus pages failed to load or were cut off before 271), so no quotation marks are used. Partial-to-strong match on timing and knowing one's hearer; Plato is describing the orator in general rather than an envoy, and he says nothing about protocol or place.

689.quote_or_event: “But I thought that I ought not to do anything common or mean in the hour of danger: nor do I now repent of the manner of my defence, and I would rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live.”
689.explanation: After being condemned, Socrates explains why he would not weep, plead or bring his children into court to win pity, saying that he would rather die than save himself with words unworthy of him.
689.tie_back: Like the Kural's envoy, Socrates holds that no pressure, even the threat of death, should force a shameful word from a man of firm character.
689._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett). Partial match: the shared point is firmness against saying anything base under threat. Socrates is defending himself, however, not carrying a king's message to other kings.

696.quote_or_event: “He, therefore, added one more to the number of those who have shown to their bitter cost how little kings care for their friends' good advice.”
696.explanation: Seneca tells how Praexaspes advised King Cambyses to drink less, and the drunken king shot the adviser's son through the heart to prove his hand was steady. Seneca judges that Praexaspes was wiser in holding his tongue afterwards than in offering correction to such a king in the first place.
696.tie_back: The tale shows the danger the Kural guards against, which is giving a king sound but unwelcome advice without reading his mood or waiting for the right moment.
696.source: Seneca, De Ira (Of Anger), III.14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
696._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart translation, Book III). Partial match: it is a cautionary example of ill-timed counsel to a king, not a positive teaching on timing and pleasing speech. Seneca's main concern in the chapter is controlling anger.

698.quote_or_event: “Duties are universally measured by relations. … In this manner, therefore, you will find, from the idea of a neighbor, a citizen, a general, the corresponding duties if you accustom yourself to contemplate the several relations.”
698.explanation: Epictetus teaches that what we owe someone follows from the role or relation in which they stand to us, such as father, brother, citizen or general, and not from what we think of them personally.
698.tie_back: In the same way the Kural asks that the king be treated according to the office he holds, not according to his age or his kinship with oneself.
698._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter translation). Partial match: the shared principle is that the role sets the duty. Epictetus does not discuss rulers who are younger than oneself or related to one, which is the Kural's specific case.

700.quote_or_event: “… who with his own hand while at table stabbed Clitus, his dearest friend, who had been brought up with him, because he did not flatter him enough, and was too slow in transforming himself from a free man and a Macedonian into a Persian slave.”
700.explanation: Seneca recalls how Alexander killed Clitus, a friend he had grown up with, at a banquet for speaking too freely, and how he caged Lysimachus, another close friend, with a lion.
700.tie_back: Clitus' fate shows the Kural's warning in action: an old intimacy with a king did not protect the friend who took liberties in his presence, and it led to his ruin.
700.source: Seneca, De Ira (Of Anger), III.17 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
700._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart translation, Book III). Next-best partial match: the event fits the Kural closely, but Seneca condemns Alexander's anger rather than Clitus' over-familiarity, so the moral is drawn from the opposite side.

715.quote_or_event: “In all cases, then, silence is a safe adornment for the young man, and especially so, when in listening to another he does not get excited or bawl out every minute, but even if the remarks be none too agreeable, puts up with them, and waits for the speaker to pause …”
715.explanation: Plutarch advises a young man attending a philosopher's lecture to listen in silence, to wait until the speaker has finished, and not to rush in with objections, recalling the saying that nature gave us two ears and one tongue.
715.tie_back: Plutarch, like the Kural, praises the restraint of a younger person who does not hurry to speak before those wiser than himself.
715.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On Listening to Lectures (De auditu), ch. 4 (tr. F. C. Babbitt)
715._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Babbitt, Loeb Moralia vol. I, 1927). Strong match on a young person's restraint in speech before a more learned speaker; the Kural's ranking of this restraint as the best of all goods is not paralleled.

719.quote_or_event: “Never call yourself a philosopher, nor talk a great deal among the unlearned about theorems, but act conformably to them. … Thus, therefore, do you likewise not show theorems to the unlearned, but the actions produced by them after they have been digested.”
719.explanation: Epictetus tells the student not to lay out philosophical principles before people who cannot receive them, but to keep silent among them and show the fruit of those principles in conduct.
719.tie_back: Both texts hold that worthy teaching should not be spoken before an audience unfit to receive it.
719._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter translation). Strong match on not speaking good things to an unfit audience. Epictetus' reasons are humility and the risk of speaking undigested doctrine, rather than the unworthiness of the assembly as such.

738.quote_or_event: “We may define happiness as prosperity combined with virtue; or as independence of life; or as the secure enjoyment of the maximum of pleasure; or as a good condition of property and body, together with the power of guarding one's property and body and making use of them.”
738.explanation: In his guide for political speakers, Aristotle sets out the commonly agreed parts of happiness, including wealth, health and the secure enjoyment of life, and applies several of them to whole communities as well as to individuals.
738.tie_back: Aristotle's list of what makes life good overlaps closely with the Kural's ornaments of a country, which are health, wealth, happiness and security.
738.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, I.5, 1360b (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
738._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Rhys Roberts). Partial match: Aristotle's list is mainly of an individual's happiness, and harvests are absent, but health, prosperity, enjoyment and security all appear, and the chapter applies some of them to states.

819.quote_or_event: “… when he has been deceived by the pretences of the other person, it is just that he should complain against his deceiver; he will complain with more justice than one does against people who counterfeit the currency, inasmuch as the wrongdoing is concerned with something more valuable.”
819.explanation: Aristotle says the bitterest complaints between friends arise when one pretended to love the other for his character while really loving him for profit or pleasure, and he ranks this deception above counterfeiting money.
819.tie_back: Aristotle, like the Kural, treats a friendship in which outward profession differs from the real disposition as a grievous wrong.
819.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, IX.3, 1165b (tr. W. D. Ross)
819._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross). Strong match on the wrong of a friend whose show differs from his reality. Aristotle contrasts pretended and real motives rather than words and deeds, and the Kural's image of the pain reaching even into dreams is absent.

820.quote_or_event: “The dissembler is a man, for instance, who accosts his enemies and engages readily in talk with them, to show that he bears no grudge, and who praises to their faces the very men he slanders behind their backs …”
820.explanation: In the first of his character sketches, Theophrastus describes the dissembler, who is friendly in private encounters while running the same people down elsewhere.
820.tie_back: This is almost exactly the person the Kural warns against: friendly in private and disparaging in public.
820.source: Theophrastus, Characters, I (The Dissembler) (tr. Charles E. Bennett and William A. Hammond)
820._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Bennett and Hammond translation (1902) on Project Gutenberg (eBook #58242). Near one-to-one description of the type; Theophrastus describes the character but, unlike the Kural, gives no explicit command to avoid him.

865.quote_or_event: “Your enemy, wide awake, is constantly lying in wait to take advantage of your actions, and seeking to gain some hold on you, and keeping a constant patrol about your life …”
865.explanation: Plutarch says an enemy watches every action for a fault to seize on, and he urges that this watchfulness be turned to profit by living so carefully that the enemy finds nothing to use.
865.tie_back: Read from the other side, Plutarch's point matches the Kural's: a person who neglects right conduct, propriety and shame hands his watching enemies exactly what they want.
865.source: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Profit by One's Enemies (De capienda ex inimicis utilitate), ch. 3 (tr. F. C. Babbitt)
865._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Babbitt, Loeb Moralia vol. II, 1928). Partial match: Plutarch states the positive lesson (live blamelessly because enemies are watching), whereas the Kural describes the negligent man who delights his enemies; the four specific failings are not listed.

868.quote_or_event: “Therefore the bad man does not seem to be amicably disposed even to himself, because there is nothing in him to love; so that if to be thus is the height of wretchedness, we should strain every nerve to avoid wickedness and should endeavour to be good; for so and only so can one be either friendly to oneself or a friend to another.”
868.explanation: Aristotle argues that a wicked man, having nothing lovable in him, is at odds with himself and cannot be a true friend to others. In the next chapter he adds that bad men cannot hold together in common purpose.
868.tie_back: This supports the Kural's claim that a man without virtues and full of faults ends up without allies.
868.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, IX.4, 1166b (tr. W. D. Ross)
868._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross). Strong match on vice leaving a man friendless; Aristotle does not draw the Kural's further strategic conclusion that this friendlessness strengthens his enemies.

882.quote_or_event: “There are no intrigues more difficult to guard against than those which are concealed under a pretence of duty, or under the name of some intimate connection. For you can easily avoid one who is openly an adversary, by guarding against him; but this secret, internal, and domestic evil not only exists, but even overwhelms you before you can foresee it or examine into it.”
882.explanation: Accusing Verres of betraying the consul he served as quaestor, Cicero argues that the treachery of a trusted associate is far more dangerous than open hostility.
882.tie_back: Cicero makes the Kural's own contrast: an open enemy can be guarded against, while an enemy in the guise of a friend or kinsman strikes before he is detected.
882.source: Cicero, Against Verres (In Verrem), II.1.39 (tr. C. D. Yonge)
882._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseids/Perseus (Yonge, The Orations of Marcus Tullius Cicero, vol. 1, 1903). Near one-to-one match of the open-enemy versus hidden-enemy contrast; the source is a forensic speech rather than a philosophical treatise.

891.quote_or_event: “Now slighting is the actively entertained opinion of something as obviously of no importance. … clearly you do not think that he can do you harm, for then you would be afraid of him instead of slighting him …”
891.explanation: Aristotle defines anger as a painful impulse to revenge for an unjustified slight, and observes that we slight only those we judge unable to harm us; if we thought them capable, we would fear them instead.
891.tie_back: To belittle someone is to misjudge his power, and the Kural's first safeguard is never to make that error about people who are able to act.
891.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, II.2, 1378b (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
891._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Rhys Roberts); spacing artefacts in the online text normalised. Next-best partial match: Aristotle analyses slighting and the anger it provokes, and he does not himself give the Kural's prudential warning against belittling capable people.
